findings.q: How many club players come back the next season, and does it differ by division?
findings.hyp: Season-to-season retention is well under 100% and lower in the women’s division, where squads are smaller and more teams fold.
findings.method: Every player on a club roster in a season (first/second teams, masters) counted as back if they appear anywhere the next season: any club, any format, GB squads included. Division = the division they mostly played that season.
findings.result: Across everyone, 75% of 1078 club players from 2025 are seen again in 2026 (provisional: the season is still being recorded). Open: 78%; Mixed: 73%; Women: 71%. Of players who missed exactly one season, 25% came back the season after (176 of 712); after two missed seasons 20% (68 of 349).
confounds: “Back” means seen at the events and squads we track. A player who dropped to a club that only plays Tour, or to pickup, counts as gone.
Roster coverage grew each year (more Instagram squad lists from 2024), so early seasons understate who was around and overstate churn.
gaps: UKU membership records would say who is still registered but not playing the tracked events.
A leaver survey for the one-season-missed group, who are the ones most likely to come back.

findings.q: Of the players who first appear in a given season, how many are still playing one, two and three seasons later, and does the club they started at change that?
findings.hyp: Most loss happens in the first year or two; players who start at a strong club stay longer (they were selected, and they get more games).
findings.method: Entry cohorts = first season seen on a club roster, 2022–2025. Survival = share seen at or after each later season. Starting club tier from the team level of their club that first season. The 2022 cohort includes everyone already playing (data starts there), so it is a mix of new and established players.
findings.result: Pooling cohorts, 76% are still playing one season on and 68% two seasons on (n=1530). top club (level 70+): 84% after one season · mid club (40–69): 84% after one season · lower club (under 40): 70% after one season.
confounds: Selection: strong clubs pick players who were already committed; the club tier is a marker, not a cause.
The 2022 “cohort” is really everyone we first saw, including long-time players; true newcomers are only separable from 2023.
Later cohorts have had less time, so pooled horizons mix cohorts.
gaps: Year each player actually started ultimate (survey or membership join date) would turn this into a real entry-cohort analysis.
University and school rosters would show the pipeline before the first club season.

findings.q: Do players leave soon after their best season, or play on past their peak?
findings.hyp: Most leavers go within a season of their peak Quality: people stop while still good, not after a long decline.
findings.method: Players with 3+ scored seasons. Peak = the season with their highest Quality. For those not seen in 2026, seasons between peak and last appearance. Anyone whose last season is 2025 is a provisional leaver: the 2026 season is still being recorded, so the “gone while good” list is the group to check on now, not a verdict.
findings.result: Of 96 leavers with 3+ scored seasons, 23% were last seen in their peak season and 57% within a season of it. 8 left in their best season with Quality 50+ (the “gone while good” group); 179 with Quality 50+ have played on 2+ seasons past their peak.
confounds: 3+ seasons is required to have a peak, so this is about players who already stayed a while.
Quality tracks the team’s results as much as the player, so a peak can be the club’s good year.
Only four scored seasons exist (2022–26), which caps how far after a peak anyone can be.
gaps: Reason for leaving (injury, moved abroad, work, family, lost interest) from an exit survey. This group is the one to ask.

findings.q: Do players who only play one kind of event drop out more than players who play the full season?
findings.hyp: Players whose season is only Tour, or only Nationals, are less attached and leave more; players who travel to European events are the most committed.
findings.method: Each club player-season classified by the events they played that year; share seen again the next season.
findings.result: Played in Europe: 86% back (n=1780) · Tour + Nationals: 68% back (n=669) · Nationals only: 62% back (n=200) · Tour / Regionals only: 68% back (n=236) · Invites only (no UKU event): 29% back (n=255)
confounds: Commitment and ability run together: the players who go to Europe are also the better players at stronger clubs.
Tour-only players include many on second teams whose next season may be at a club we track less well.
gaps: Local leagues, indoor leagues and pickup are invisible here; a Tour-only player who moves to league play looks like a leaver.

findings.q: Does the number of events a player plays in a season predict whether they come back?
findings.hyp: A dose–response: each extra event in a season raises the chance of being seen next season, with diminishing returns.
findings.method: Events played per club player-season (distinct tournaments, GB events excluded) against the share back next season.
confounds: Reverse direction: players who were already leaving play fewer events in their last season.
Event counts depend on which tournaments we hold rosters for; a club that posts no Tour squads undercounts.
gaps: Attendance at training, not just tournaments, would separate “plays a lot” from “travels a lot”.

findings.q: Do players who change clubs stay in the sport longer or shorter than players who stay put, and does the direction of the move matter?
findings.hyp: A move up keeps people in; a move down is often the step before leaving.
findings.method: Three cuts. (1) Players on a club roster in two consecutive seasons, split by whether they changed club between them, and whether they were seen a season later: both groups had the same chance to move. (2) Players with 3+ club seasons, by how many club changes they made, and whether they are still playing in 2026. (3) Every club move with both team levels known, by direction, and whether the player was seen the season after.

rows.label: Stayed at the club between two seasons: seen a season later
Changed club between two seasons: seen a season later
0 club moves (3+ club seasons): still playing
1 club move (3+ club seasons): still playing
2 club moves (3+ club seasons): still playing
3+ club moves (3+ club seasons): still playing
After a move up (stronger team): back next season
After a move level (similar level): back next season
After a move down (weaker team): back next season

findings.result: Stayed at the club: 83% seen a season later (n=1265) · Changed club: 84% seen a season later (n=299). Among players with 3+ club seasons: 0 moves: 83% still playing (n=395) · 1 moves: 89% still playing (n=237) · 2 moves: 87% still playing (n=70) · 3+ moves: 100% still playing (n=16). back after a move level: 85% (n=72) · back after a move down: 74% (n=137) · back after a move up: 91% (n=149)
confounds: Moving takes effort: people who bother to find a new club are already the committed ones, so moving is a marker of commitment as much as a cause of staying.
Moves down include relocations and life changes we cannot see.
A player who moved to a club we hold no rosters for looks like a leaver.
gaps: Why people moved (relocation, selection, friends, cost) from a short survey of recent movers.

findings.q: When players switch division, where do they go, what happens to their Quality, and do they stay?
findings.hyp: Open → Mixed is the common late-career step and extends careers; Mixed → Open/Women is the step up for improving players and costs Quality at first.
findings.method: Consecutive seasons where a player’s main club division changed (masters excluded). Mean change in Quality across the switch and share seen the season after.
findings.result: Mixed → Open: 114 players, Quality -1.4, 87% back · Women → Mixed: 79 players, Quality +1.5, 80% back · Mixed → Women: 74 players, Quality +9.2, 88% back · Open → Mixed: 73 players, Quality +8.1, 87% back
confounds: Quality is division-relative (100 = top of that division), so a switch moves the yardstick as well as the player.
Mixed squads are larger and more clubs run one, so Mixed is also where people land when their open or women’s team folds.
gaps: The reason for the switch: team folded, selection, friends, wanting to play with a partner. Ask recent switchers.

findings.q: Is dropout concentrated at the bottom (weak clubs, low Quality) or does it happen at every level?
findings.hyp: Loss is heaviest at the bottom and much lower for established players at strong clubs.
findings.method: Share back next season by the player’s club tier that season and by their Quality band.
findings.result: mid club (40–69): 82% · lower club (under 40): 70% · top club (level 70+): 83%. By Quality: under 30: 66% · 30–49: 83% · 50–69: 89% · 70+: 96%
confounds: Low-Quality players are also the ones with the least roster evidence, so some “leavers” are players we simply stopped seeing.
Quality rises with events played, which is itself a retention signal (see the dose finding).
gaps: Membership status for the under-30 group to tell lapsed from gone.

findings.q: Does the quality a club gains or loses through moves in one season predict how its rating changes the next?
findings.hyp: Net quality in (arrivals’ Quality minus leavers’ Quality) leads the club’s rating by a season.
findings.method: For each club-season with 2+ moves in or out and a rating in both that season and the next: net Quality flow against the rating change to the following season. Spearman correlation.

chart.xlabel: net Quality in through moves (season N)

findings.result: Spearman ρ = 0.12 across 78 club-seasons: a weak lead
confounds: Ratings move for many reasons (who turns up to Nationals, the field that year); moves are one input.
Most moves involve mid-Quality players, so the flow number is dominated by volume, not star power.
gaps: More seasons. Four seasons of ratings is the limiting factor here, not the method.

findings.q: Which events draw the strongest players, and how far apart are they?
findings.hyp: WUCC and EUCF sit well above Nationals, which sits above Tour; the Europe-wide tour events sit between.
findings.method: Mean Quality of the players on rosters at each kind of event (one count per player per event), 2022–2026.
findings.result: Elite Invite: 67 (n=572) · EUCF: 60 (n=1164) · WUCC: 54 (n=573) · Spring Tour: 42 (n=1005) · Tom's Tourney: 40 (n=645) · UKU Nationals: 39 (n=3066) · Summer Tour: 37 (n=1163) · Windmill: 34 (n=304) · UKU Tour / Regionals: 30 (n=3373)
confounds: Quality itself rewards finishing well at these events, so the ordering is partly built in. The size of the gaps is the information, not the order.
gaps: Game scores at Tour and Nationals would let the rating, not placings, set the level.

findings.q: Do GB squads drawn mostly from one club, or with many returning players, finish higher?
findings.hyp: A core from one strong club (shared systems) and more returning caps both help; squads spread thinly across many clubs finish lower.
findings.method: Every GB squad with 10+ known players and a finish: share from the single biggest club, number of clubs, share of new caps, against finishing place (lower is better). Spearman within senior, U24 and junior lines.

chart.xlabel: share of squad from its biggest club

findings.result: Senior: ρ(top-club share, place) = -0.49, ρ(new caps, place) = -0.12 over 6 squads · U24: ρ(top-club share, place) = -0.36, ρ(new caps, place) = 0.38 over 6 squads. Negative ρ = more concentration / more new caps goes with a better finish.
confounds: One squad per edition: n is tiny and the field changes every time (Worlds vs Euros, who else entered).
Club share is read from the squad list’s club column, which is missing for many older squads.
gaps: Game-by-game results for GB squads (WFDF has them) would replace a single place with a strength measure.

findings.q: How old are GB youth products when they reach a senior squad, and when they stop playing?
findings.hyp: Youth entrants reach senior squads around 22–25 and most are gone from the tracked game by 30.
findings.method: No birthdates exist in the data. For players who were in a GB U17, U20 or U24 squad, the age band of that squad gives a birth year to within ±1–2 years (narrowed when they appear in more than one youth squad). Ages below use the midpoint.

keys.name: Age at first senior GB squad
Age of those still playing in 2026

findings.result: 750 players have a birth-year estimate. Median age at first senior squad 23 (n=100); median age when last seen, for those who reached club ultimate and have gone since 2022, 26 (n=79); those still playing club ultimate are a median 24 (n=267).
confounds: Only GB youth products have an estimate, and they are the most committed players of their age; this says nothing about the typical club player’s age.
The estimate is ±2 years for most players.
gaps: Birth year (or even age band) on membership would allow relative-age-effect analysis across the whole sport: the standard talent-development question, which we cannot touch today.

findings.q: Do GB players stay in the sport more than club players of the same standard?
findings.hyp: GB selection adds commitment beyond ability: at the same Quality band, GB players come back more.
findings.method: Share back next season by Quality band, split by whether the player had been in any GB squad by that season.

keys.key: GB squad that year or before
keys.name: Has been in a GB squad

findings.result: under 30: GB 86% vs non-GB 65% · 30–49: GB 84% vs non-GB 82% · 50–69: GB 92% vs non-GB 87% · 70+: GB 97% vs non-GB 93%
confounds: Quality includes a GB selection term, so GB players sit higher in a band by construction.
GB players have more roster evidence (squad pages), so they are easier to “see” next season.
gaps: Training-squad and trial lists would add the players who tried for GB and were not picked: the right comparison group.

findings.q: How big is each stage of the pipeline: youth teams, club teams, rostered players, GB youth squads?
findings.hyp: The club game is fed by a youth base we barely see and a large university game we see only as teams.
findings.method: Counts per year (2022 on, where rosters exist) of distinct teams at UKU Youth events, distinct UK club teams at UKU events, distinct players on club rosters, and GB U17/U20 squads.

head: Year
Youth teams (UKU Youth)
University teams (indoor, season ending that year)
Club teams at UKU events
Players on club rosters
GB U17/U20 squads

findings.result: 2026: 16 youth teams, 256 university indoor teams, 77 club teams, 1321 rostered players. University teams are now counted, but without players nobody can be followed from university into the club game: that is where most sports lose the most players.
confounds: Youth results only run from 2021 and name teams, not players, so nobody can be followed from youth to club.
Club team counts depend on which events we hold standings for each year.
gaps: BUCS results and university squad lists.
UKU Youth rosters, or even a count of registered junior players per year.
Membership numbers by age band and region from UKU: the one dataset that would size every stage.

cannot.q: Does relative age (birth quarter within a school year) predict GB youth selection and later retention?
cannot.why: No birthdates. The youth-squad proxy is ±2 years, far coarser than the quarter needed.
cannot.need: Birth month and year on membership, or on GB squad applications.

cannot.q: Does playing at university predict staying in the club game?
cannot.why: University results are now in (Universities section, 2021-22 on), but only as teams: university rosters are not published.
cannot.need: UKU’s JustGo roster exports for university nationals (every player is a UKU Uni member), matched to names.

cannot.q: Do captains, coaches and committee members stay longer?
cannot.why: Roles are recorded for seven people in total (five GB youth coaches, two beach captains).
cannot.need: A roles field on squad lists, or a one-question survey: “have you captained, coached or run a club?”

cannot.q: Why do people leave: injury, cost, moving, work, lost interest, bad experience?
cannot.why: Nothing in the data records a reason.
cannot.need: An exit survey sent to the “gone while good” and the one-season-missed groups this tool can list by name.

cannot.q: Does early specialisation (ultimate only, from a young age) help or hurt?
cannot.why: No record of other sports played.
cannot.need: Survey item on other sports played to age 16.

cannot.q: Are players who drop out still playing somewhere we do not look (league, indoor, pickup, abroad)?
cannot.why: Only tracked tournaments and squad lists count as “present”.
cannot.need: UKU membership renewals, indoor league rosters, or a “are you still playing?” check sent to recent leavers.

cannot.q: Does individual performance (not team results) drive selection and retention?
cannot.why: Game stats exist for only a few events (WUCC, EUCF, some Invites).
cannot.need: This data is unlikely to ever exist at scale; player stats at Nationals would be the one realistic addition.

cannot.q: Does region or travel distance to events affect retention?
cannot.why: Home location is not recorded; clubs are the only geography.

defs:
present in a season  = any appearance that year (club event, club roster list, GB squad, overseas club)
  on a club roster     = Club first/second team, Masters side, Secondary team (training players excluded)
  left after year Y    = present in Y, never seen in any later year we hold (2026 is the current season, so 2025 leavers are
                         provisional; "left" really means "not seen at the events and squads we track")
  back next season     = present in Y and in Y+1 (any club, any format)
  evidence grade       strong = large n and a clear gap that survives the obvious split; suggestive = clear gap, small n or an
                       obvious selection story; weak = pattern visible but could easily be noise or selection
